messages.subject_clean: Wanted: proof-readers !
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

right now, Andy Royle and I are finishing the writing of the 2nd volume of the Applied Hierarchical Modeling for Ecologists book project (i.e., AHM2).  Academic Press tell us that they will send us the proofs startin in the last week of August.

Now, we are looking for 1-3 additional proof-readers for each of the 12 chapters which are listed here:

12. Relative-abundance models for population dynamics
13. Modeling population dynamics while accounting for imperfect detection
14. Hierarchical models of survival
15. Modeling species distribution and range dynamics using dynamic occupancy models
16. Modeling metacommunity dynamics using dynamic community models
17. Multi-state occupancy models
18. Modeling false-positives
19. Models for species interactions
20. Spatial modeling for abundance and occupancy
21. Integrated models
22. Spatial distance sampling and spatial capture-recapture (SCR)
23. Conclusions

If you're interested in helping us and and could do the proofs for one or more chapters, please let us know. We would expect you to give a chapter one thorough read and return to us within 1 week from receipt any detected errors or serious awkwardnesses in the text.

The audience of this mail is not limited to the two Google groups to which it is sent, so if you like you can also forward to colleagues who you think might be interested.

Thank you very much.

Best regards  --- Marc & Andy

______________________________________________________________

I've attached the script of the code I used. I understand the obsCovData only has one column and I think that may be the issue, but I'm not sure how to change that. If anyone has an idea of what this error might mean, I would greatly appreciate any help!!

Thanks!!

Angie

messages.body_plain:
Hi Angie,

A noticed a couple things. In your script you are assigning both the detection history (y) and the site-specific covariates (detectionhistory.site) to the same two columns of your input dataset (detectionhistory[,2:3]). Are these columns actually detection history or actually site covariates? They shouldn't be both.

If they are supposed to be the detection history (y), then you seem to have 2 observations at each site since there are 2 columns. Also I noticed that these columns have values greater than one (are they counts?). unmarked::occu() will automatically truncate any value over 1 to 1 so that the observations can be used in an occupancy modeling framework.

Assuming again that detectionhistory[,2:3] is supposed to be the observations y, when you supply observation-level time covariate, you need exactly 1 per observation. Since you have 28 sites (# of rows of y, or M) and 2 observations per site (# of columns of y, or obsNum) your time observation covariate should be of length 56 (28*2, M*obsNum). But in your code you generate a time covariate with length 84 (28*3) instead, which results in the error you saw. Maybe you want this instead:

time<-as.factor(rep(c(1,2),n))
detectionhistory.obs<-data.frame(time)

If I do this, and also remove the site covariate data for the reason stated above, I can get the model to run:

library(unmarked)
detectionhistory <- read.csv("detection_history_sample1.csv")
y<-detectionhistory[,2:3]
n<-nrow(detectionhistory)

time<-as.factor(rep(c(1,2),n))
detectionhistory.obs<-data.frame(time)
detectionhistory.occu<-unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y, obsCovs = detectionhistory.obs)
(fit <- occu(~time~1, data=detectionhistory.occu))

However, you get a very large intercept estimate for occupancy because you don't have any sites where the species was never detected, again assuming columns 2 and 3 are supposed to be the detection history.

Ken

                          obsCovs  = obs.covs)

                          siteCovs = …,

If you want to compare detection probability models for the two seasons, then I would argue that you don't want separate analyses.  You want to create a dummy variable (or factor) that identifies the season and use the complete data set.  Otherwise you'd be throwing away information about the status of the site.

I'm assuming that because you want to use occu that the occupancy status must be identical in both seasons.  (Otherwise, if the occupancy status can different in between seasons, then you'd want to use colext.)   So if you perform separate analyses, then at a site where you have detections in one season but not the other, then you'd not be using the information in one of the analyses which would identify the true status of the site.

Here is one way (of many ways) to create an unmarked data frame identifying season and perform the desired analyses.

> # Load library
>   library(unmarked)
>
> # Get data
>   y = read.csv("det_hist_sample2.csv")
>
> # Create season 1 and season 2 observation level variables
>   nSites = dim(y)[1]
>   season1 = matrix(rep(c(1,0), nSites, each=6), nrow=nSites, byrow=TRUE)
>   season2 = matrix(rep(c(0,1), nSites, each=6), nrow=nSites, byrow=TRUE)
>   x = matrix(runif(12*nSites), nrow=nSites)
>   obs.covs = list(season1=season1, season2=season2, x=x)

> # Create unmarked data frame
> # The first column in y is a row identifier so it is skipped.
>   ufo = unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y[,-1], obsCovs=obs.covs)
>
> # Separate detection probabilities for each season
>   occu(~-1 + season1 + season2 ~1, ufo)

> # Same model as above but the P-value for season1 is associated with
> # the test of equivalent seasonal detection probabilities.
>   occu(~season1 ~1, ufo)
> >
> # Model with different slopes and intercepts by season for the covariate x
>   occu(~season1 + x + season1:x ~1, ufo)
> # Same model as above but explicitly obtaining separate estimates for each
> # slope and intercept.
>   occu(~-1 + season1 + season2 + season1:x + season2:x ~1, ufo)
>

That seems very odd.  Is it possible that the data set you were given had surveys in one season but not the other?

Jim

As a statistician it's not that I don't believe you (well, maybe that's it a little) but that in some cases having all detections in one time period and not the other (when it's not consistently the first or second time period with the detections) should cause some concern.  If the per visit detection probability is very low, then that can certainly be the case.  But is it the case here?  The per visit detection probability (ignoring any covariates) is around 0.083.  That is low.  The probability that there is at least one detection in 6 visits is around 0.4.  So the proportion of occupied sites with at least one detection in a 6-visit time period and no detections in the other 6-visit time period is around 0.48.  But your sample data set has 100% with that condition when one would expect around 48% (and the sample data set contains only sites with at least one detection).  (If you're that good at getting extreme results, please buy a lottery ticket for me.)

But my poor attempts at humor aside...If there is some condition where detection is typically found in one time period but not the other, then you'll need to model that.  Maybe that's some change-in-weather covariate unrelated to occupancy. I just don't know.  But some covariate associated with season to explain that phenomenon might be warranted.

About colext:  If occupancy might change between seasons at a site, then occu won't do.  You'll need something like colext.  This is the "closure" requirement:  occu models assume that occupancy status does not change at a site during a season.  This is critical for you to choose which analysis to use.  Your statement "The detection/occupancy is expected to differ, however, among sites and it may vary throughout the season." suggests that the closure assumption doesn't hold.

About creating "dummy variable/factor":  Separate analyses won't allow you to properly compare detection models of the two seasons.  Your estimates of the parameters might be just fine but the standard errors will likely be off (and likely too large in this case).  A very rough analogy of performing separate analyses with separate data sets would be having paired measurements but analyzing the difference with a two-sample t-test rather than the more appropriate paired t-test.  Doing so ignores the sampling design as the two time periods are matched on the same site.

About plots:  You might want to ask that question separately because it's kinda buried with all of this other stuff.  Having a fresh question I think would get you more targeted help.

Jim

messages.subject: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?
messages.subject_clean: stacked-data single-season vs. multi-season models: is the former good enough when the latter is possible?
messages.body_plain:
Greetings unmarked community,

I recently reviewed a manuscript that had clear value and represented an important contribution (I'll go light on the details for obvious reasons of confidentiality) that employed a stacked single-season abundance (N-mixture) model (via pcount) for an animal population data set with repeated within-year counts over several decades. One focus of the manuscript was on estimating (exponential) population growth rates under a variety of scenarios. To estimate growth rates, a site covariate (year) was added to model abundance, much as is commonly done in a mixed-effects Poisson or negative binomial GLM when detection is assumed (explicitly or otherwise) to be 1. There was no clear rationale for using pcount (vs. the Dail-Madsen [via pcountOpen]) model in this paper (beyond addressing detection) and there was nothing to indicated systematic issues in the data (i.e., entire years missing) required the use of a stacked single-season model.

Perhaps I'm a little too attached to open-population models as implemented in unmarked (I've published three papers using these models), but it struck me as non-trivially problematic that the authors chose to use the stacked single-season model, particularly since pcountOpen offers the "trend" dynamic to estimate growth rates from sequential years (N[i,t] = N[i,t-1]*gamma). In my understanding, this estimation of gamma (trend/growth) from year-to-year site-level changes in abundance (when data allows it) is far more robust than estimation via a year covariate in a stacked-data single-season model. I tried to state my concerns as clearly and constructively as possible and the AE is requiring the authors to respond to my concerns. However, the overall assessment by the AE (and, in turn, the ME) was that my concerns did not warrant a revision to the analysis.

I certainly don't want to "sink" a valuable analysis (not that it appears I could even if I wanted to), I'm just of the strong opinion that using multi-season models are the right tool for the job (here pcountOpen rather than pcount) when there appears no necessity to using a stacked-data model. To be clear, I don't in any way think stacked-data single-season models are "wrong" (as has been discussed and revisited; https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/unmarked/OHkk98y09Zo/6gRiEowXNeMJ), but in this case I believe there is a clear "right" way to proceed when revising this analysis (at least in a MLE framework =)).

What do you all think? Are my concerns warranted or do I just sound like an angry old man shouting at kids on my lawn? I welcome any on- or off-list responses and will try to respond with extreme care to any on-list questions.

Grateful for the unmarked community and the package developers, as always.

- Giancarlo

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Re: effective open multi-season model by stacking years (so site/years = sites)
messages.body_plain:
In general I would say you want to include year as a covariate in the occupancy calculation. IDEALLY this would be as a random effect and year would be coded as a factor, but since unmarked doesn't do random effects it has to be a fixed effect. The year factor covariate would account for some year to year variation that affects all your points equally. Where there could be issues is if there is a trend or some other year to year influence that is important to your conclusions or to study system in some way that "interferes" with the interpretation of another variable. You may want to check colinearity of all your variables and see if any have high colinearity with year (and in a more general sense this should always be done in any regression model). E.g. if one of your variables has a strong trend across years it may be difficult to interpret the model fit when both that variable and year are included in the same model. The "vif" statistic from package HH is one good way to do this.

Alternatively, you can code year as a numerical value and then it accounts for linear trend in your data. If that makes sense for your study then I think it is appropriate.

In conclusion, the answer (to a great many stats questions as it turns out) is: it depends. It is my opinion that year can be included in a subset of the models you are evaluating as long as you have good reason to do so. I have run occupancy models using stacked data without year as a covariate when I had other variables that happened to be colinear with year (e.g. climate data).

Is there a name for the pairwise comparisons above?

For example in the literature I see pairwise comparisons like:

we used Tukey’s pairwise comparison
we used Tukey's honestly-significant-difference test to make pairwise comparisons

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabriella,

It's unclear to me what you mean when you say you didn't detect one of the species at the station. In your y matrix for a given species, a value of 1 should represent that the species was detected at station i in occasion j, 0 means it was not detected at that station-occasion, and NA means you didn't sample during that station-occasion (which is different than not detecting the species). If you have NA for all occasions at a particular station you are telling occuMulti that you didn't sample at that station at all (or all the data was lost or something), and it therefore can't be used to help fit the model. This is true even if you have some non-missing values for other species at that station - if all occasions are NA at a station for any 1 species, you can't use that station.

Some unmarked functions drop a site with all missing values automatically but right now occuMulti does not. You would have to manually remove those stations (5,7..etc) from your dataset before you input them into your unmarkedFrame.

Ken

Hi Laura,

I think there are two issues. First, when doing backtransform/linearComb, your first command works because you are providing one coefficient value (i.e., for the intercept) for type='det', which matches because your detection model in fm80 is intercept-only. For your second linearComb command, you are providing 5 values in your coefficients argument but type is still 'det'. Maybe you mean for argument type to be 'state' instead, since your occupancy model has an intercept + 4 covariates?

More importantly though, your selected model fm80 did not converge (as unmarked has warned), and your parameter estimates are very large and very uncertain. I would not trust any inference/prediction from the model and suggest exploring why your model isn't converging, perhaps starting by trying to fit a simpler occupancy model (maybe intercept-only) and working your way back up to the more complex models.

Ken

Lack of convergence issues much of the time requires looking at the data rather just the output to figure out what's going on.  If you're willing to share the data, then more targeted help can be found.

If you don't want to or can't share the data with everyone on the list, that is very understandable.  Sharing an appropriate subset of the data might alleviate some concerns but if lack of convergence is an issue, then usually all of the data is needed.

If you're willing to share the data just certain with individuals, then all folks that I know on this list abide by the same rules:  (1) we share your data with no one else and (2) any responses once the data is shared with an individual just goes to you and not the list.  If you want to share any of those responses, then that's up to you.  However, you sharing good responses is certainly encouraged.

I'd be happy to look at the data and let you know what I see.

I'd also echo what Ken Kellner wrote.  The convergence issue should be fixed first.  (While the standard errors are on the same order as the estimates, it just might be that none of the variables have much effect given the others in the model and maybe some of the predictor variables are highly correlated with each other.  Again, it's hard to say without the data.)

The second issue would be stating in words what you want rather than just giving the code.  For example, do you want to make predictions of occupancy probabilities given specific values of the predictor variables? Do you want odds ratios?

Jim

Hello,

I am a master's student in the crux of thesis crunch time. I have been working on intpretting the results of my code, and am finding some troubling numbers. Due to studying elusive species over the short duration of a master's, these numbers aren't going to be friendly to begin with. But they seem completely off for some of the species I am analyzing.

In addition, general interpretation--e.g. how literature discusses these values, is not innately obvious.

Data: I have site and observational covariates; have to run each possible combination (assigned as fm_#). Then a model selection table is run in order to find the "best fit" for each species.

For this example, the "best fit' is fm_6:
Call:
occu(formula = ~Habitat_classification + Basal_area_hectare ~
    Trap_days, data = umf)

Occupancy:
            Estimate     SE      z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)   0.4568 1.9765  0.231   0.817
Trap_days    -0.0115 0.0201 -0.571   0.568

Detection:
                                                            Estimate   SE              z            P(>|z|)
(Intercept)                            -                9.061  17.1896       -0.52714 0.598096
Habitat_classificationLess Disturbed   -8.118   881.9583    -0.00921 0.992656
Habitat_classificationMore Disturbed 12.423  17.2109        0.72180 0.470416
Basal_area_hectare                            -0.136    0.0408       -3.32993 0.000869

AIC: 86.63837

As you can see, these values are ridiculous. This is the only run that has come out with values of this sort. For other species who have fm_6 as their best fit model, their values are still not this high. This species is particularly challenging to detect; however, these high SE values are concerning.

Additionally, I am hoping to receive clear insight on how to report these values. Based on the literature, it seems common place to report the k, AIC (or AICc in my case), delta AIC, psi, SE psi, chi sq, p value, and c-hat. I have the test statistics from the Mackenzie Bailey package; it is the psi and SE psi values that I believe I'm not interpreting correctly. Thanks for your help!

OK.  I'm a statistician so I have to ask such questions.  (And if one's major professor/supervisor insists on certain things, I don't have any constructive suggestions about that.)

So under the assumption that the code is fine one can look at the model results.  For occupancy one can estimate the probability of occupancy for various numbers of trap days, say 0 and 14.  That gives estimates of

> 0.6122548 = 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.4568))  (for zero trap days)
> 0.5734155 = 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.4568 - 0.0115*14))  (for 14 trap days)

So there isn't much of a range meaning the estimate of the probability of occupancy is around 0.6 (and I'm assuming that maybe 14 days is a maximum amount of trap days).  And the variable "Trap_days" is not even close to being statistically significant so I'm a little surprised that "Trap_days" made it into the top model.

For detection:  I'm assuming that Habitat_classification:Less Disturbed, Habitat_classification:MoreDisturbed, and Basal_area_hectare are all site variables (i.e., they don't change over visits).  I don't know what the range of basal_area_hectare values are but my guess is that the numbers range from 0 to 1000. Hi Mark,

That `newformatLong` function was a custom function that's not included in the example and likely doesn't work any more even if you had it. The current `formatLong` function is to be preferred, and I don't suspect `visit` is a yearlySiteCov.

You'll need to modify your `visit` variable to reflect your primary/secondary sampling scheme. You have 10 possible visits to a site (5 primary periods, each with 2 secondary samples), so `visit` would need to take values in 1:10 across all sites. That is, primary period 1 (2014) with be associated with visits 1 & 2, primary period 2 (2015) will be associated with visits 3 & 4, and so on.

I've not intensively checked this, but the following should set up your data to be ready for `formatLong`:

library(unmarked)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

FWCPdata <- read.csv("~/FWS_Projects/sandbox/Data/FWCPDataLongTsp.csv", header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
  # Drop records with no response; we'll complete data set below
  filter(!is.na(y))

# Explicitly define the sampling scheme so we can complete the data set with missing values later
sampling_scheme <- expand.grid(spp.6 = unique(FWCPdata$spp.6),
                               visit = 1:10,
                               site = unique(FWCPdata$site),
                               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

FWCPdata <- FWCPdata %>%
  arrange(spp.6, site, date) %>%
  mutate(date = dmy(date), # Convert string to date
         doy = yday(date), # Day of year variable; I think this is what you want instead of the 'Julian' function
         year = lubridate::year(date),
         visit = visit + ((year - min(year)) * 2 )) %>% # Number visits assuming 5 primary (yearly), 2 secondary periods
  # Use sampling scheme to fill the data set with NAs, keeping the visit sequence correct
  left_join(sampling_scheme, .) %>%
  # Rearrange columns for unmarked
  select(site, visit, y, spp.6, place.1:doy) %>%
  # Rearrange rows for human eyes
  arrange(spp.6, site, visit)
